title: Removing the Thorns
era: Mauryan period (c. 4th–3rd century BCE, traditional dating)
tale: Book IV of Kautilya's Arthashastra is called Kantakashodhana — 'the removal of thorns'. It covers the policing of fraudulent artisans and merchants, and the detection of crime through spies, circumstantial evidence and careful questioning.
lesson: A good judge follows the evidence — the smudge on the lid — not the easiest suspect.

title: The Weights of Harappa
tale: Indus cities used remarkably standardised cubical weights, often cut from chert. The smaller weights double at each step (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64…) while larger ones follow a decimal pattern — the same standard across hundreds of kilometres.
lesson: Honest trade needs a shared standard that anyone can check.
source: Archaeological finds at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Lothal

title: Rani ki Vav, the Queen's Stepwell
tale: This great stepwell descends seven levels into the earth and is lined with hundreds of carved sculptures. It is traditionally credited to Queen Udayamati, in memory of King Bhima I of the Chaulukya dynasty. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
lesson: Water shared well becomes a monument; water fought over becomes a feud.

title: Whose Tree?
era: Mughal period folk tradition (16th century setting)
tale: In a well-loved folk tale, two men claim one mango tree. Birbal has each told at night that thieves are raiding it. The true owner rushes out to protect what he has tended; the pretender does not stir.
lesson: Test what people do, not only what they say.

title: The Envoy Megasthenes
tale: Megasthenes, envoy of the Seleucid king Seleucus I, lived at the court of Chandragupta Maurya and wrote the Indica. It survives only in quotations by later writers, describing the great wooden walls of Pataliputra and the city's administration.
lesson: Foreign visitors bring trade and ideas — and carry away knowledge of your realm.
source: Fragments of Megasthenes' Indica, preserved by Strabo, Arrian and others

title: The Superintendent of Elephants
tale: The Arthashastra names a Superintendent of Elephants and describes protected elephant forests guarded by foresters. Elephants were counted among the greatest assets of an army, able to break gates and scatter formations.
lesson: What is precious to the realm should be protected and paid for, not simply seized.

title: The Shorter Line
tale: Akbar drew a line and asked his courtiers to shorten it without touching it. They were baffled until Birbal drew a longer line beside it.
lesson: Sometimes you change a thing by changing what surrounds it.

title: Sugar and Sand
tale: Challenged to separate sugar from sand, Birbal scattered the mixture beside an anthill. By morning the ants had carried away the sugar and left the sand.
lesson: Know who in your realm is best suited to each task.

title: The Hall Full of Light
tale: Asked to fill a room completely at almost no cost, the wise answer was not straw or sand but a single lamp, whose light reached every corner.
lesson: Small, well-chosen measures can reach an entire realm.

title: The Institution of Spies
tale: The Arthashastra describes spies disguised as students, recluses, householders, merchants and ascetics. It advises that information be believed only when separate sources agree.
lesson: Check one report against another before you act on it.

title: Harsha's Assembly at Prayag
tale: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described how King Harshavardhana held a great assembly at Prayaga every five years and gave away the wealth stored in his treasury to monks, Brahmins, the poor and the needy.
lesson: A treasury exists to serve the people in their hour of need.
source: Xuanzang, Records of the Western Regions

title: The Great Wall of Kumbhalgarh
tale: Built under Rana Kumbha, Kumbhalgarh is ringed by walls said to run for about 36 km over the Aravalli hills. It is one of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan listed by UNESCO, and the traditional birthplace of Maharana Pratap.
lesson: Walls hold only when every gate is watched.
source: UNESCO World Heritage listing, Hill Forts of Rajasthan (2013)

title: Todar Mal's Survey
tale: Raja Todar Mal, Akbar's finance minister, reorganised land revenue from 1580 by measuring fields and setting the tax from the average produce and prices of the previous ten years (the dahsala system).
lesson: Fair taxation begins with honest measurement.

title: Kallanai, the Grand Anicut
tale: Tradition credits the Chola king Karikala with building the Kallanai, a stone weir across the Kaveri that diverts its waters into the fertile delta. It is still in use today — among the oldest water-regulation works in the world that still function.
lesson: A king who tames the river feeds generations yet unborn.
source: Tamil Sangam-era tradition; Public Works records of the Kaveri delta

title: Ashoka's Roadside Trees
tale: In his Seventh Pillar Edict, the emperor Ashoka records that he had banyan trees planted along the roads for shade, mango groves grown, wells dug and rest-houses built for people and animals.
lesson: Care for the traveller is care for the whole realm.

title: Sher Shah's Road
tale: In a reign of only five years, Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and extended the great road from Bengal to the north-west, later called the Grand Trunk Road, with sarais at regular intervals and a horse-post for messages. He also issued the silver rupiya.
lesson: Roads, rest-houses and reliable coin bind a realm together.

title: Upadha: Testing the Ministers
tale: The Arthashastra advises the king to test each minister in secret with four kinds of temptation — righteousness (dharma), wealth (artha), desire (kama) and fear (bhaya) — and to give each post only to those who withstand the relevant test.
lesson: Trust is earned under temptation, not in comfort.

title: Kautilya and the Arthashastra
tale: Tradition identifies Kautilya with Chanakya, the counsellor of Chandragupta Maurya. The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics and law, was rediscovered in manuscript by R. Shamasastry in Mysore in 1905 and translated into English in 1915.
lesson: Statecraft is the art of seeing clearly — including what others hide.
